summary: Circulates an implementors' guide for the ISO Transport Protocol to the Internet community for comment. It collects practical advice for building implementations of that protocol. The RFC says it may not relate directly to Internet research but could interest implementors.

eli5.summary: It is a tips-and-tricks booklet for people building the ISO transport rules into real machines, to help them avoid common mistakes.

subtitle: Practical guidance for building the ISO Transport Protocol

tldr.problem: The ISO Transport Protocol standard (IS 8073) is formally described using Estelle, a specification language that is abstract and general but does not directly map to implementation decisions, making it difficult for implementors to understand how to adapt the formal description to their operating environment.
tldr.mechanism: This memo explains how to interpret the formal description's mechanisms and abstractions, discusses general approaches to implementing the protocol, and provides guidance on handling specific features like timers, flow control, and different transport classes.
tldr.outcome: Implementors can build efficient, robust ISO Transport Protocol implementations tailored to their network environment while remaining conformant to the standard.

today: RFC 1008 remains a valuable reference for implementors of ISO TP (TP4) used in some legacy systems and certain specialized networks. The transport protocol is now less commonly deployed than modern alternatives like TCP/IP, but the implementation guidance is relevant to anyone building protocol stacks. The distinction between formal specification and practical implementation remains central to protocol design.

sections.title: About This Guide
sections.content:
This RFC circulates an implementors' guide for the ISO Transport Protocol (IS 8073) to members of the Internet research community for comment. The ISO Transport Protocol is a layer four (transport) protocol in the ISO Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model, providing reliable, ordered delivery of data over various network services.

The formal description of the protocol uses Estelle, a formal description technique based on state machines and process algebra. Estelle allows precise specification of protocol behavior, but it is intentionally abstract: it expresses all behavior that implementations must demonstrate without specifying how any particular implementation would achieve that behavior within a specific operating environment. This abstraction is essential for supporting diverse networks and platforms, but it leaves implementors with many questions about how to efficiently realize the formal mechanisms in their systems.

This guide explains the intent behind the formal description and offers practical advice for interpretation and implementation, drawing on the authors' experience implementing and testing the protocol.
sections.eli5: The ISO Transport standard is written in a very formal language that describes what the protocol must do, but not exactly how to code it. This guide helps implementors understand what the formal description means and how to turn it into working code.

sections.title: Protocol Structure
sections.content:
The ISO Transport Protocol entity (TPE) is structured as a collection of modules interacting through Estelle channels. The Transport Protocol Machines (TPMs) represent the endpoints of individual transport connections. One TPM per connection manages connection establishment, data transfer, and closure. The Network Slave module handles output to the network, managing queues and providing downward flow control. The TPE itself manages network connections, resource allocation, and integrity checking of received data.

The formal description includes six classes of transport protocol: General (for connection negotiation), Class 0 (basic, no error recovery), Class 1 (recovers from network failures), Class 2 (multiplexing with flow control), Class 3 (optional), and Class 4 (full error recovery with checksums and timers). In practice, most implementations focus on Class 2 and Class 4, with Class 2 usable as a simplified Class 4 by disabling certain features.

Critical to implementation is understanding that the Estelle structure expresses formal relationships and synchronization constraints, not necessarily how processes should be scheduled. In many operating environments, the TPE and TPMs can run in parallel (contrary to the Estelle scheduling), providing better performance while maintaining the same semantic guarantees.
sections.eli5: The transport protocol is split into modules: one for each connection (the TPM), one for sending data to the network (the Slave), and one manager (the TPE). The formal description says they must synchronize in a certain way, but real code might arrange them differently as long as the results are the same.

sections.title: Interpreting Formal Mechanisms
sections.content:
The formal description uses several mechanisms that must be adapted to the operating environment. Timers are expressed as spontaneous transitions with a delay parameter in Estelle. Implementors should not implement all timers literally but instead select the simplest and most efficient timing mechanism for each case. Some timers need high accuracy (like retransmission timeouts), while others tolerate significant delays (like connection cleanup); using different mechanisms for each improves overall performance.

The formal description uses spontaneous transitions to express nondeterministic events that may happen at unpredictable times. For example, a Class 4 connection might attempt to obtain a new network connection at any time if all current connections have disconnected. Rather than checking conditions frequently and executing these transitions literally, implementors should use appropriate mechanisms: timeouts for time-driven actions, interrupts for network events, and deferred procedures for housekeeping tasks.

Another key mechanism is the channel abstraction, which represents communication paths between modules. The formal description semantics are that an interaction placed on a channel moves instantaneously to a queue at the other end. Real implementations map channels to appropriate data structures: queues, buffers, or function calls, depending on whether modules run in parallel, in the same thread, or in interrupt handlers.
sections.eli5: The formal description uses abstract concepts like "spontaneous events" and "channels." Real code should implement these using whatever works best in the operating system: interrupt handlers for asynchronous events, buffers for communication between threads, or function calls if running single-threaded.

sections.title: Service Access Points and Flow Control
sections.content:
The protocol defines two types of service access points: Transport Service Access Points (TSAPs) where users connect, and Network Service Access Points (NSAPs) where the protocol connects to the underlying network. A single transport entity may have multiple TSAPs (for example, one TSAP for high-throughput file transfer, another for low-latency interactive sessions) and multiple NSAPs (for different network technologies like X.25, Ethernet, or satellite).

The formal description models TSAPs and NSAPs using Estelle interaction points indexed by address, but real implementations typically use tables or other data structures mapped by reference numbers. Similarly, flow control is abstracted in the formal description but must be realized using mechanisms appropriate to the operating system: semaphores, signal handlers, or boolean flags shared with user code.

An important issue is how to provide addressing to users so they can reference the transport interface. The standard does not fully specify this, so implementors must develop mechanisms for communicating T_addresses and Transport Connection Endpoint Identifiers (TCEP_ids) to users, perhaps through system calls, socket APIs, or environment variables.
sections.eli5: The protocol has entry points where users connect (TSAPs) and where it connects to networks (NSAPs). The formal description describes these abstractly, but real code must implement them using whatever addressing and flow control mechanisms the operating system provides.

sections.title: Transport Classes and Implementation Strategies
sections.content:
The protocol defines different classes for different reliability needs. Class 2 provides multiplexing and flow control over reliable network services (like X.25). Class 4 adds error recovery, checksums, and timers for use over unreliable services (like IP datagram networks). The formal description separately describes Class 0 and 1 as well, but most implementations focus on Class 2 and 4. A practical strategy is to implement Class 4 fully and derive Class 2 from it by disabling checksums, timers, and retransmission logic.

For efficiency, implementors should merge the General TPM (which handles connection negotiation) with the Class 2 and Class 4 TPMs, using variables to control class-specific behavior. The formal description's separation is for clarity, not a requirement on implementation structure. Similarly, TPDU processing should be optimized: header encoding/decoding can use separate functions per TPDU type (as the formal description does) or a single parameterized function, depending on clarity and efficiency trade-offs.

An important consideration is the representation of data. The formal description assumes that user data can be arbitrarily long, modeling it as a file pointer. Real implementations might stream data through, accumulate it in buffers, or support both modes. The choice depends on memory constraints, latency requirements, and network characteristics.
sections.eli5: The protocol comes in different versions for different reliability levels. Class 4 is the most robust but slowest; Class 2 is lighter and faster. Smart implementations build Class 4 fully and create Class 2 by turning off the extra safety features, rather than coding both separately.

sections.title: Performance and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The formal description is not optimized for performance; it is designed for clarity and generality. Implementors should apply optimization strategies: execute TPMs in parallel with the TPE (not strictly serialized); avoid literal implementation of all spontaneous transitions (use system timers instead); minimize context switching and scheduling overhead; and manage memory dynamically for connection tables and queues rather than allocating fixed maximum sizes.

For operational systems, two criteria guide the realization of formal mechanisms: minimize delays caused by the mechanism itself (transit delay for channels, access latency for shared variables, scheduling delay for timers) and minimize handling overhead per invocation (context switching, synchronization protocols, predicate evaluation). On connectionless network services (like IP), the principal implementation challenge is buffering at the NSAP, especially at high data rates. Implementations should monitor network behavior, computing mean transmission delays for timer adjustment and exerting backpressure on connections when network loading rises.

The memo also notes that to achieve high communication rates, protocol implementation must reside in the kernel or at high priority in the OS, since these layers run on behalf of many clients, run frequently, and execute for brief periods. User-space implementations will suffer from scheduling and context-switching overhead. Some implementors may benefit from ethernet-style broadcast or multicast optimization, though this is noted as an open research area.
sections.eli5: The formal description is not the fastest way to code the protocol. Real implementations should use kernel-level timers instead of checking conditions constantly, run different parts in parallel when possible, and manage memory dynamically to adapt to the network and load.
